p1.key: BF3 and SO3 have three bonding domains and no lone pair on the central atom: trigonal planar, 120°. NCl3 has a lone pair, so it is trigonal pyramidal (about 107°): I and III only.
Carbons 1 and 2 have four single bonds (four electron domains): sp<sup>3</sup>. Carbon 3 in COOH has a C=O double bond (three domains): sp<sup>2</sup>. sp needs a triple bond or two double bonds.
H2O forms hydrogen bonds; H2S does not, so H2S has the lower b.p. In A and C the second substance is larger (stronger London forces); in D ethanol has H-bonding and so the higher b.p.

Oxidising an alkanol (C—OH, sp<sup>3</sup>) to a carboxylic acid (C=O, sp<sup>2</sup>) changes the hybridization. In A the carbon stays sp<sup>3</sup>; in B and C the carbonyl carbon stays sp<sup>2</sup>.
XeF4 has 6 electron domains (4 bonds and 2 lone pairs), so it is square planar. SiCl4, BF4− and NH4+ each have 4 bonding domains and are tetrahedral.
Bond order affects length: C=C in ethene (0.134 nm) is shorter than the delocalized 1.5-order bonds in benzene (0.140 nm), which are shorter than C—C in ethane (0.154 nm): I < III < II.
CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> is polar (bent C—O—C), so it has dipole–dipole forces as well as London (van der Waals') forces. It cannot hydrogen bond with itself because no H is bonded to O.
O<sub>2</sub> is O=O, CO<sub>2</sub> is O=C=O, and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> has a C=C bond: all three contain a double bond.

H<sub>2</sub>O has two lone pairs, which repel more strongly than bonding pairs and squeeze the angle to about 104.5°. NH<sub>3</sub> (one lone pair) is about 107°, CH<sub>4</sub> 109.5° and H<sub>2</sub>CO about 120°.
The C≡N carbon has two electron domains: sp. The CH<sub>2</sub> carbon has four single bonds: sp<sup>3</sup>. The COOH carbon has a C=O: sp<sup>2</sup>.

Ring carbons in benzene are sp<sup>2</sup>. In methylbenzene the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon is sp<sup>3</sup>. COOH and CH=CH<sub>2</sub> carbons are sp<sup>2</sup>, and the C≡N carbon is sp, so only C has both sp<sup>2</sup> and sp<sup>3</sup>.
BF<sub>3</sub> is trigonal planar (120°). CF<sub>4</sub> is 109.5°, NF<sub>3</sub> (one lone pair) about 107° and OF<sub>2</sub> (two lone pairs) about 104°.

In the ethanoate ion, CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>, the negative charge and π electrons are delocalized over both C—O bonds (resonance), making them equal in length. In ethoxide the C—O is a single localized bond.
CF<sub>4</sub> is tetrahedral, with all angles 109.5°. PF<sub>5</sub> (trigonal bipyramidal) and SF<sub>6</sub> and SiF<sub>6</sub><sup>2−</sup> (octahedral) all contain 90° angles.
Highest vapour pressure means the weakest intermolecular forces. The ether C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> cannot hydrogen bond with itself, while the alcohol, acid and amine all can.
Weak intermolecular forces need little energy to separate the molecules, so both the boiling point and the enthalpy of vaporization are low. Strong forces give high values of both.

HF has the largest electronegativity difference (H 2.2, F 4.0), so it is the most polar. F<sub>2</sub> is non-polar, HCl has a smaller difference, and CF<sub>4</sub>'s symmetric tetrahedral shape cancels its bond dipoles.

Propan-1-ol has an OH group that hydrogen bonds with water, and only a short non-polar chain. Pentan-1-ol has a longer hydrocarbon chain, so it is less soluble. Alkanes cannot hydrogen bond with water.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F. Alkanols (O—H) and amines (N—H) both have this. Alkanals, esters and bromoalkanes have no such H, and hydrocarbons have only London forces.
CO<sub>2</sub> linear 180° > BF<sub>3</sub> trigonal planar 120° > CH<sub>4</sub> tetrahedral 109.5° > SF<sub>6</sub> octahedral 90°.

N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> (H<sub>2</sub>N—NH<sub>2</sub>) has an N—N single bond, which is the longest. N<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> have N=N double bonds, and N<sub>2</sub> has a triple bond, the shortest.

Both C atoms in ethene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) are sp<sup>2</sup>. Ethane's carbons are all sp<sup>3</sup>. C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> is ambiguous: propene has two sp<sup>2</sup> C and one sp<sup>3</sup> C, while cyclopropane is all sp<sup>3</sup>. So ethene is the only species that is wholly sp<sup>2</sup>.
p1.flag: ambiguous: C3H6 isomer unspecified; removed from marking

p1.key: O<sub>3</sub>, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> and CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> are all resonance hybrids with delocalized π electrons. In H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> the S=O and S—OH bonds are localized because the H atoms fix the structure.
S in SO32− has four electron domains (3 bonding, 1 lone pair): the electron domains are tetrahedral but the shape is trigonal pyramidal, with the angle reduced to about 107° by the lone pair.
Halogen molecules are non-polar, so only London (dispersion/van der Waals') forces act between them. These increase with the number of electrons, so boiling points rise down the group.
Carbon monoxide has a C≡O triple bond, which is the shortest C–O bond. CO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CHO have C=O double bonds, and ethanol has a single C–O bond.

The six ring carbons each have three electron domains (delocalized π system), so they are sp<sup>2</sup>. The nitrile carbon (C≡N) has two electron domains, so it is sp. There are no sp<sup>3</sup> carbons.

In ethoxide, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>O⁻, the charge sits on one O with only single bonds, so there is no π system to delocalize. Ethanoate, O<sub>3</sub> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> all have resonance structures with delocalized π electrons.

All are C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub> with the same number of electrons. Straight-chain hexane has the largest surface contact between molecules, so its London forces are strongest. Branching makes molecules more compact and lowers the boiling point.
H–C(=O)–O–CH3: bond pairs = H–C, C=O (2), C–O, O–C and 3 C–H = 8. Each oxygen has 2 lone pairs, so there are 4 lone pairs.
The central carbon in CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> forms a double bond, so it has three electron domains (trigonal planar). The C–C–C angle is about 120°.

SO<sub>2</sub> has two equivalent resonance structures (S=O and S–O swapping places), so its π electrons are delocalized. CO<sub>2</sub> and HCOOH (neutral acid) have localized double bonds; TiO<sub>2</sub> is largely ionic.
The central I in I3− has 5 electron domains (2 bonding, 3 lone pairs). The lone pairs take the equatorial positions of the trigonal bipyramid, so the ion is linear.
Strong intermolecular forces need more energy to overcome, so the enthalpy of vaporization is large and the boiling point is high.
Ethanoic acid has an –OH group, so its molecules hydrogen bond to each other (forming dimers). The ether, ketone and chloroalkane only have dipole–dipole and London forces.
CO<sub>2</sub> is a linear, non-polar molecule, so only London (van der Waals') forces act between its molecules. Covalent bonds are within molecules, not between them.

All have 4 electron domains around N. NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> has 2 lone pairs (~105°), NH<sub>3</sub> has 1 (~107°), NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> has none (109.5°). Lone pairs repel more strongly, so more lone pairs means a smaller angle.

(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–CH=CH–C≡C–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>: two CH<sub>3</sub> and the CH are sp<sup>3</sup> (3); the two C≡C carbons are sp (2); the four C=C carbons are sp<sup>2</sup>, so there are four sp<sup>2</sup> carbons, not three. I and III are correct.
F–F is a non-polar bond (identical atoms), while H–F is polar because F is much more electronegative. So only HF is a polar molecule.

p1.key: Ethanal contains C–H and C–C single bonds and a C=O double bond. It has no H bonded to O, N or F, so its molecules do not hydrogen bond to each other (only dipole–dipole and London forces).

p1.key: Ethane (C–C), ethene (C=C), ethyne (C≡C): the number of shared pairs between the carbons and the bond strength increase, while bond length decreases.

p1.key: PCl<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is tetrahedral (109.5° only). PCl<sub>5</sub> is trigonal bipyramidal (90° between axial and equatorial bonds) and PCl<sub>6</sub><sup>−</sup> is octahedral (90°).

p1.key: In graphite and C<sub>60</sub> each carbon bonds to three others with delocalized π electrons (sp<sup>2</sup>). In diamond each carbon bonds tetrahedrally to four others (sp<sup>3</sup>).

p1.key: Delocalization gives benzene extra stability, so it substitutes (keeping the ring intact) rather than adding. It also makes all C–C bonds equal in length (between single and double). Comparing combustion and hydrogenation enthalpies gives no evidence.

p1.key: Electronegativity differences: B–C 0.6, C–O 0.8, N–O 0.4, O–F 0.6. C–O has the largest difference, so it is the most polar.

CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> have three bonding domains and no lone pair on the central atom: trigonal planar. SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> has a lone pair on S, so it is trigonal pyramidal, not planar.
Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water and has a short non-polar chain. Ethane cannot H-bond, methoxymethane only accepts H-bonds, and butan-1-ol's longer hydrocarbon chain lowers its solubility.

N in NH<sub>3</sub> has four electron domains (three bonds, one lone pair): tetrahedral electron domain geometry, so sp<sup>3</sup>, but the molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal because the lone pair is not counted in the shape.
Sigma bonds form by end-on overlap, which can involve s orbitals, p orbitals (or hybrids). Pi bonds need sideways overlap of p orbitals; s orbitals are spherical and cannot form pi bonds.

CO<sub>2</sub> has two electron domains (two double bonds) and no lone pairs on C, so it is linear. SO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>S and Cl<sub>2</sub>O have lone pairs on the central atom and are bent.

NH<sub>3</sub> molecules form hydrogen bonds (N–H with a lone pair on N), which are much stronger than the dipole–dipole and London forces between PH<sub>3</sub> molecules. PH<sub>3</sub> actually has stronger London forces (larger molar mass).
SO<sub>3</sub> is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so its bond dipoles cancel. H<sub>2</sub>CO, CHCl<sub>3</sub> and NF<sub>3</sub> have dipoles that do not cancel.
NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> has three electron domains around N (trigonal planar) → sp<sup>2</sup>; NH<sub>3</sub> has four domains (three bonds + a lone pair) → sp<sup>3</sup>.

CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> and CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> have delocalized π electrons (resonance), so their C–O bonds are equal. CH<sub>3</sub>COOH has a distinct C=O and C–OH, so its bonds differ.

Delocalization stabilizes benzene, so its hydrogenation releases less energy than predicted for a cyclohexatriene with three C=C bonds. Benzene has one H environment, equal C–C bonds, and prefers substitution.
Vaporization separates molecules, so only intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds and London/van der Waals’ forces) are overcome. The covalent bonds within each molecule stay intact.
A double bond is one σ and one π bond. The π bond comes from weaker sideways overlap of p orbitals, so it is weaker than a σ bond; a double bond is still stronger than a single bond.

Diamond has no delocalized electrons and is the poorest conductor (I). Graphite and C<sub>60</sub> carbons each bond to three atoms and are sp<sup>2</sup> (II). C<sub>60</sub> contains pentagons as well as hexagons, so III is wrong.
Covalent bonds (hundreds of kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) are far stronger than hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than van der Waals’ (London) forces between molecules of similar size.
VSEPR theory uses the repulsion between electron domains around a central atom to predict the shapes and bond angles of molecules and ions.
NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> has two resonance structures (I). N has one lone pair, not two, plus two bonding domains: three domains, so sp<sup>2</sup> (III) and a bent shape.

PBr<sub>3</sub>, like NH<sub>3</sub>, has three bonding pairs and one lone pair on the central atom (group 15), so it is trigonal pyramidal. GaI<sub>3</sub> and BF<sub>3</sub> (group 13) are trigonal planar.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F. Only CH<sub>3</sub>OH has an O–H bond. In CH<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CHO the H atoms are bonded to carbon.

Fluorine is a small non-polar molecule with weak London forces, so it has the lowest boiling point and is most volatile. Chlorine has stronger London forces; the ionic solids have very high boiling points.
PF<sub>5</sub> is trigonal bipyramidal: equatorial F–P–F angles are 120°, axial–axial is 180°, and axial–equatorial angles are 90°, the smallest.

The two carbons in the C=C double bond each have three electron domains (sp<sup>2</sup>); the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon has four single bonds (sp<sup>3</sup>). sp would need a triple bond or two double bonds.

Halogen molecules are non-polar, so only London (dispersion) forces act between them. Down the group molecules have more electrons, so larger temporary (instantaneous) dipoles form and boiling point rises. Bond enthalpy (A) concerns intramolecular bonds, not boiling.

Ethanol dissolves as neutral molecules (hydrogen bonding with water) and does not ionize, so the solution does not conduct. HCl and NaCl give ions; ethanoic acid partially ionizes, so it conducts weakly.
H<sub>2</sub> is a non-polar molecule, so the only intermolecular forces are London dispersion (van der Waals') forces. Covalent bonds are intramolecular; H-bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F.
I in ICl4⁻ has 7 + 1 = 8 valence electrons: 4 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = 6 electron domains (octahedral). The lone pairs sit opposite each other, giving a square planar shape.
In CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH the three chain carbons have four single bonds (sp³); the COOH carbon has a C=O double bond (sp²). There is no triple bond, so no sp carbon.
Bond length decreases as bond order increases: C≡C (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>) < C=C (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) < C–C (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>).

BF<sub>4</sub>⁻: 4 domains, tetrahedral, 109.5°. BF<sub>3</sub>: 3 domains, trigonal planar, 120°. BF<sub>2</sub>⁺: 2 domains, linear, 180°. Increasing angle: BF<sub>4</sub>⁻, BF<sub>3</sub>, BF<sub>2</sub>⁺.

XeF<sub>4</sub>: Xe has 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs (6 domains, octahedral arrangement); the lone pairs are opposite each other, so the shape is square planar. XeO<sub>4</sub> and SiF<sub>4</sub> are tetrahedral; SF<sub>4</sub> is see-saw.
In H<sub>2</sub>N–NH<sub>2</sub> each N has 3 bonds + 1 lone pair (4 domains): sp³. In HN=NH each N has a double bond, a single bond and a lone pair (3 domains): sp².
In CO<sub>3</sub>²⁻ the carbon has three electron domains (one C=O and two C–O, no lone pairs), so the ion is trigonal planar with O–C–O angles of 120°.
More shared pairs pull the atoms closer: N≡N (N<sub>2</sub>) is shortest, then N=N (N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>), then N–N (N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>).
I in ICl<sub>4</sub>⁻ has 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs (6 domains). The lone pairs are opposite each other, giving a square planar shape with 90° Cl–I–Cl angles.
An sp² atom has three hybrid orbitals arranged trigonal planar, so three σ bonds at 120° (the unhybridized p orbital can form a π bond).
Strong intermolecular forces need more energy to separate the molecules, giving a large enthalpy of vaporization and a high boiling point.
Benzene burns (combustion) and, because the delocalized ring is very stable, undergoes substitution rather than addition (e.g. nitration). It has no –OH group, so it cannot undergo dehydration.
Hexane contains only C–C and C–H bonds (very small electronegativity difference), so it is non-polar. Water, propanone and ethanol all have polar O–H or C=O bonds giving net dipoles.
Bond length decreases with bond order: N≡N in N<sub>2</sub> is shortest, then N=N in N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>, then N–N in N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>.
N in NO<sub>3</sub>⁻ has three electron domains and no lone pairs, so the ion is trigonal planar with 120° bond angles.
P in PF<sub>5</sub> has five bonding pairs and no lone pairs (5 electron domains), so the molecule is trigonal bipyramidal.
C in CCl4 has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs: tetrahedral, sp³. Each Cl has 3 lone pairs, so 4 × 3 = 12 lone pairs in the Lewis structure.

HF molecules form hydrogen bonds (H bonded to highly electronegative F), which are much stronger than the London/dipole–dipole forces between other HX molecules. Boiling breaks intermolecular forces, not the covalent H–F bond, so A is wrong.
HCl(g) consists of neutral molecules with no mobile ions or electrons, so it does not conduct. Al(s) has delocalized electrons, and molten Al2O3 and KCl(aq) contain mobile ions. D.
Bond polarity depends on electronegativity difference. In a C–C bond both atoms are identical, so the difference is zero and the bond is non-polar. C.
Every carbon in H2C=CH–CH=CH2 forms a double bond and has three electron domains (trigonal planar), so all are sp2 hybridized.
PF5 (trigonal bipyramidal) has 90° axial–equatorial angles and SF6 (octahedral) has 90° angles. SiCl4 is tetrahedral (109.5°). B: I and III only.
CH4 and SiH4 are non-polar (London only), and SiH4 has more electrons so it boils higher. CH3Cl adds dipole–dipole forces, and CH3OH forms hydrogen bonds (highest). D.
H3O+ has four electron domains around O (three bonding pairs, one lone pair), so it is trigonal pyramidal like NH3, about 107°. 104.5° is for water, which has two lone pairs.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F. Propanone, CH3COCH3, has only C–H bonds, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond with each other. The amine, acid and alcohol all can. B.
In diamond each C bonds to 4 others (tetrahedral). In graphite and C60 each C bonds to 3 others, with the fourth electron delocalized. B.
In SiO2 each Si has four single bonds (tetrahedral) and each O has two single bonds plus two lone pairs, i.e. four electron domains. Both are sp3.
Carbon monoxide has a C≡O triple bond, the shortest and strongest carbon–oxygen bond here. CO2 and the C=O in CH3COOH are double bonds, and ethanol has a single C–O bond. D.
CH3OCH3 and CH3CH2OH have the same M, but only ethanol has O–H so only ethanol can hydrogen bond, giving it the higher b.p. B, C and D each put the compound with stronger intermolecular forces first.

CO is a polar molecule (O more electronegative than C), so it has dipole–dipole attractions as well as London (van der Waals') forces, which all molecules have. It has no H, so no hydrogen bonding. B.
σ bonds form by end-on (axial) overlap, and π bonds by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals. σ bonds can form from s, p or hybrid orbitals, not just s orbitals, so II is false. B.
In C60 each carbon bonds to three others with delocalized electrons: sp2. Diamond and 2-methylbutan-1-ol have only sp3 carbons; propyne has sp and sp3 carbons.
In CO, O donates a lone pair to C to form the third bond of C≡O. In H3O+, O donates a lone pair to H+. NH3 has only normal covalent bonds. B: I and III only.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F. Only ethanol, CH3CH2OH, has an O–H bond. The ether and aldehyde have O but no O–H, and propane has no electronegative atom. B.

CH2Cl2 is tetrahedral but with two different kinds of substituent, so the bond dipoles do not cancel: it is polar. BCl3 (trigonal planar) and CCl4 (tetrahedral) are symmetrical; Cl2 has no bond dipole.
Five electron domains give a trigonal bipyramid. The three lone pairs take the equatorial positions (to minimize repulsion), leaving the two F atoms axial at 180°: linear.
(CH3)2C=CClCH2CH3 is C6H11Cl, 18 atoms. In an acyclic molecule every pair of bonded atoms has one σ bond, so there are 18 − 1 = 17 σ bonds (the C=C contributes one σ and one π).

Y (3.4) and Z (4.0) are both highly electronegative non-metals; a difference of 0.6 gives a polar covalent bond. W and X are both metals (low electronegativity) and would not form an ionic compound together.
In CO, O donates a lone pair to C to form the third bond. In H3O+, O donates a lone pair to H+. Methanal (HCHO) has only ordinary covalent bonds. C: II and III only.
SF6 has six bonding pairs and no lone pairs: octahedral. XeF4 has six domains but two are lone pairs, so the molecule is square planar. PCl5 is trigonal bipyramidal and BF3 trigonal planar.

CO32− (I) and O3 (II) each have resonance structures in which the π electrons are spread over the O atoms, so they are delocalized. In methanoic acid (III) the C=O and C–OH bonds are distinct and localized. A.
Every single bond is σ; a triple bond is 1σ + 2π. Propyne has 4 C–H, 1 C–C and the C≡C: σ = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6, π = 2.

In ethoxide, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>O⁻, the charge sits on a single O with no adjacent π bond, so there is no resonance. Ethanoate, ozone and nitrate all have resonance structures with delocalized π electrons.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F. Only ethanol has an O–H group. CH<sub>3</sub>CHO and (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N have O or N but no H attached to them.
S in SO2 has three electron domains (two bonding, one lone pair), so the electron-domain geometry is trigonal planar and the molecular shape is bent (≈117°).
Stronger intermolecular forces need more energy to separate the molecules, giving a larger enthalpy of vaporization and a higher boiling point.
Bond strength increases with bond order: C–C (ethane) < C=C (ethene) < C≡C (ethyne). So the order is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>.

S in SO<sub>2</sub> has two bonding domains and one lone pair. B in BF<sub>3</sub>, P in PCl<sub>5</sub> and Si in SiF<sub>4</sub> use all their valence electrons in bonds, so they have no lone pairs.
Single bonds are σ; C≡C is 1σ + 2π. Propyne: 4 C–H + 1 C–C + 1 (from C≡C) = 6 σ, and 2 π from the triple bond.
Propene, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, has one localized C=C bond and no resonance structures. Nitrate, nitrite and ozone each have equivalent resonance structures with delocalized π electrons.

In benzoic acid every ring carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, and the COOH carbon (with its C=O) is also sp<sup>2</sup>. Methylbenzene and the alkenes in C and D contain CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>2</sub> carbons that are sp<sup>3</sup>.
Weak intermolecular forces need little energy to overcome, so both the boiling point and the enthalpy of vaporization are low.
Polarity depends on the electronegativity difference. Halogen electronegativity increases I < Br < Cl < F, so bond polarity increases H–I < H–Br < H–Cl < H–F.

Carbon (diamond/graphite) is a covalent network, so a lot of strong covalent bonds must break: high melting point. CO<sub>2</sub> is a simple covalent molecule held by weak London forces: low melting point.

All are similar molecules; going from ethane to iodoethane the number of electrons increases, so London forces get stronger, and the halogenoethanes are also polar. Boiling points increase CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> < C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl < C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br < C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>I.
In diamond each C forms four σ bonds (sp<sup>3</sup>). In graphite and in C<sub>60</sub> each C bonds to three others with a delocalized π system, so both are sp<sup>2</sup>; III is false.

CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> cannot hydrogen bond with itself, so its intermolecular forces are weaker than in ethanol and it evaporates more easily. Higher temperature also raises vapour pressure, so methoxymethane at 30 °C is highest.
The C in H<sub>2</sub>CO has three electron domains (two C–H and one C=O, a double bond counting as one) and no lone pairs, so the shape is trigonal planar.

Br<sub>2</sub> is non-polar, so its only intermolecular forces are London (van der Waals') forces from temporary dipoles. H<sub>2</sub> cannot hydrogen bond, and NH<sub>3</sub> hydrogen bonds so its forces are stronger than those in PH<sub>3</sub>.
"Like dissolves like": non-polar octane and methane mix with non-polar hexane through London forces. Water is polar and hydrogen bonded, so it does not dissolve in hexane.
In I the p orbitals are parallel and overlap sideways above and below the axis: a π bond. In II they point at each other and overlap end-on along the axis: a σ bond.

Benzene has a delocalized π ring and ozone has resonance between two equivalent structures. In CH<sub>3</sub>COOH the C=O and C–OH are distinct, so its π electrons are localized (unlike the ethanoate ion).
CO has a triple bond, one of which is dative (both electrons from O). In H<sub>3</sub>O⁺, H⁺ accepts a lone pair from O to form a dative bond. NH<sub>3</sub> has only normal covalent bonds.
Bond polarity depends on the electronegativity difference: O–H = 3.4 − 2.2 = 1.2, C–O = 0.8, S–H = 0.4, C–H = 0.4. O–H is the most polar.
α: O has two bonds and two lone pairs, bent ≈104.5°. β: ring carbon has three electron domains, ≈120°. θ: the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon has four bonding domains, tetrahedral ≈109.5°.

All molecules have London (van der Waals') forces. HBr and CH<sub>3</sub>F are polar, so they also have dipole–dipole forces; Cl<sub>2</sub> is non-polar. CH<sub>3</sub>F cannot H-bond because its H atoms are bonded to C, not F.

Each single bond is σ and each double bond is 1σ + 1π: σ = 46 + 5 = 51, π = 5. The O has two bonds and two lone pairs (four domains), so it is sp<sup>3</sup>. The OH is on a CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, so retinol is a primary alcohol.

SO<sub>2</sub> is bent because of a lone pair on S, so the S=O bond dipoles do not cancel and the molecule is polar. In linear CO<sub>2</sub>, trigonal planar SO<sub>3</sub> and tetrahedral CCl<sub>4</sub> the bond dipoles cancel by symmetry.
HI is a polar molecule, so it has dipole–dipole forces, and London forces act between all molecules. There is no hydrogen bonding because H is not bonded to N, O or F.

SF<sub>4</sub> has 5 electron domains (4 bonds + 1 lone pair): a see-saw shape. The lone pair pushes the bonds together, so the axial F–S–F angle is slightly under 180° (~173°, so α measured round the outside is ~187°) and the equatorial angle β is under 120° (~103°).

Ozone has two resonance structures, with π electrons delocalized over all three O atoms, and benzene has a delocalized π ring. Ethanal has a single localized C=O double bond, so it has no delocalization.

The alcohols (A, B) form hydrogen bonds, so their boiling points are high. Of the two C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> alkanes, the branched, compact (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>C has less surface contact, so it has weaker London forces and the lowest boiling point.

ClF is formed from two non-metals with a small electronegativity difference (about 0.8), so its bonding is predominantly covalent. LiCl is ionic, and Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and ZnCl<sub>2</sub> are mainly ionic with some covalent character.
Si and SiO<sub>2</sub> are both giant covalent (network) structures. Melting them means breaking many strong covalent bonds, so both have high melting points.

ClF<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> has 6 electron domains around Cl (4 bonds + 2 lone pairs). The lone pairs sit opposite each other, giving a square planar shape. CF<sub>4</sub> and BF<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> are tetrahedral, and SF<sub>4</sub> (one lone pair) is see-saw.

Atom 1 (CH<sub>3</sub> carbon) has 4 single bonds, so it is sp<sup>3</sup>. Atom 2 (carbonyl C) has 3 electron domains including the C=O, so it is sp<sup>2</sup>. Atom 3 (OH oxygen) has 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs, so it is sp<sup>3</sup>.
SiO<sub>2</sub> is a giant covalent network. Each Si is tetrahedrally bonded to 4 O atoms and each O bridges 2 Si atoms, giving the 1 : 2 formula. There are no discrete SiO<sub>2</sub> molecules.

The three compounds have similar molar masses (44–46 g mol<sup>−1</sup>). Propane has only London forces, ethanal (polar C=O) adds dipole–dipole forces, and ethanol forms hydrogen bonds. Boiling point order: propane < ethanal < ethanol.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCOOH contains 6 C–H/O–H bonds (5 C–H + 1 O–H), 3 C–C, 1 C–O and 2 double bonds (C=C, C=O). Every bond has one σ, so there are 11 σ bonds. Each double bond adds one π, so there are 2 π bonds.
NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> and CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> each have resonance structures, so their π electrons are delocalized across the ion. Propanone has a single localized C=O bond.

Water forms extensive hydrogen bonding (two H atoms and two lone pairs per molecule), so the most energy is needed to separate its molecules. NH<sub>3</sub> forms weaker hydrogen bonding, and H<sub>2</sub>S and CO<sub>2</sub> have only weaker forces.

H<sub>2</sub>Se is bent and polar, but Se is not N, O or F, so it has London and dipole–dipole forces but no hydrogen bonding. CO is slightly polar, so it has London and dipole–dipole forces. Non-polar H<sub>2</sub> has London forces only.

In [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>, each H<sub>2</sub>O donates a lone pair to Fe<sup>3+</sup>. In NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, the N lone pair forms a dative bond to H<sup>+</sup>. H<sub>2</sub>O itself has only ordinary covalent bonds.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C≡CCH<sub>2</sub>COOH has 7 C–H, 1 O–H, 5 C–C (including the σ of C≡C), 1 C–O and 1 C=O bond. That is 15 σ bonds. The triple bond has 2 π bonds and C=O has 1, giving 3 π bonds.

X is a benzene ring carbon with 3 electron domains, so it is sp<sup>2</sup>. Y is the alcohol O, with 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs, so it is sp<sup>3</sup>. Z is the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon, with 4 single bonds, so it is sp<sup>3</sup>.

The carboxylic acids form hydrogen bonds (and dimers), so they have far stronger intermolecular forces than the alkanes. Propanoic acid is larger than ethanoic acid, so it also has stronger London forces and the highest enthalpy of vaporization.

Y and Z are both highly electronegative non-metals with a small difference (0.6), so they share electrons covalently. W and X are both metals with low electronegativity, so they bond metallically (an alloy), not ionically or covalently.

Ethyne has a C≡C triple bond and ethene a C=C double bond. More shared electron pairs give a shorter, stronger bond, so C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> has the shorter bond length and the greater bond strength.

A very high melting point means strong bonds throughout the structure. It is insoluble in water and does not conduct even when molten, so there are no ions or delocalized electrons. This points to a giant covalent (giant molecular) structure such as SiO<sub>2</sub>.
A σ bond forms by end-on (axial) overlap along the bond axis: p with p head-on (II) or s with p (III). Side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals (I) gives a π bond.
The sulfate ion (I) and ozone (III) can each be drawn as several equivalent resonance structures, so their π electrons are delocalized. Ethanal (II) has one localized C=O bond.
At any temperature B has a lower vapour pressure than A, so B's molecules escape the liquid less easily. This means B has stronger intermolecular forces (and a higher boiling point, so C is wrong).
p1.flag: vapour pressure curves not explicit in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: In carbon monoxide, C≡O, one of the three bonds is a coordinate bond in which both electrons come from oxygen. HCN, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> contain only ordinary covalent bonds.
Bond length decreases as bond order increases: N≡N (in N2) is shortest, N=N (in N2H2) is intermediate and N–N (in N2H4) is longest: N2 < N2H2 < N2H4.
Liquid ammonia molecules are held by hydrogen bonds (H bonded to N), which are broken when it boils. A and B break covalent bonds; H<sub>2</sub> has only London forces.
CH2=CH–C≡N: σ bonds = 3 C–H + 1 C=C + 1 C–C + 1 C≡N = 6; π bonds = 1 (in C=C) + 2 (in C≡N) = 3. Every single bond is σ; a double bond has 1 π, a triple 2 π.

Benzene (ring of delocalized π electrons), carbonate (resonance over three C–O bonds) and graphite (delocalized electrons between layers) all have delocalization. Propanone, CO<sub>2</sub> and ethyne have only localized bonds, ruling out A, B and D.
Valence electrons: 2 C × 4 = 8, 3 H × 1 = 3, 2 O × 6 = 12, plus 1 for the negative charge: 8 + 3 + 12 + 1 = 24. Forgetting the charge gives 23.

NH<sub>3</sub> donates its lone pair to H<sup>+</sup> from HF, forming NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>F<sup>−</sup>; the new N–H bond is a coordinate bond. The other pairs lack an electron-pair donor plus a suitable acceptor (CH<sub>4</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> and Cl<sub>2</sub> do not accept pairs).

Pentane has only London forces (lowest b.p.); butan-1-ol has hydrogen bonding; propanoic acid hydrogen bonds more strongly (it can form dimers, with a more polar O–H), so it is highest: pentane < butan-1-ol < propanoic acid.

Glucose is a simple molecular substance (low m.p., no ions so does not conduct when molten) with many –OH groups that hydrogen bond to water, so it is very soluble. CCl<sub>4</sub> is insoluble; SiO<sub>2</sub> has a very high m.p.; molten NaCl conducts.
PCl5 has five bonding domains and no lone pairs on P, giving a trigonal bipyramidal shape with angles of 90° (axial–equatorial), 120° (equatorial) and 180° (axial–axial).

Carbon atoms with three electron domains (one double bond or delocalized ring) are sp<sup>2</sup>: ethene (C=C) and benzene. Butane, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, has only single bonds, so its carbons are sp<sup>3</sup>.

A Lewis structure must show all valence electrons, including the three lone pairs on each F. Diagrams II and III do this (dots and crosses are interchangeable). Diagram I shows only the bonds, with no lone pairs, so it is not a complete Lewis structure.
p1.flag: No markscheme; answer depends on whether I (bonds only, no lone pairs) is accepted

p1.key: Butane has only London forces (lowest); propanone adds dipole–dipole forces; both alcohols hydrogen bond. Propan-1-ol is unbranched, giving greater surface contact than propan-2-ol, so it is highest: butane < propanone < propan-2-ol < propan-1-ol.
Xe in XeF4 has 6 electron domains (4 bonding, 2 lone pairs) arranged octahedrally. The lone pairs sit opposite each other, so the molecule is square planar with 90° F–Xe–F angles.

α is a benzene ring carbon (3 domains, delocalized π) so sp<sup>2</sup>; β is the C=O carbon of the amide, also sp<sup>2</sup>. γ is the –OH oxygen with 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs (4 domains), so sp<sup>3</sup>.

CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> is tetrahedral but has two different kinds of substituent (H and Cl), so the bond dipoles do not cancel and the molecule is polar. CO<sub>2</sub> (linear) and CCl<sub>4</sub> (symmetric tetrahedral) have cancelling dipoles; C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> is non-polar.

Carbonate (resonance across three C–O bonds) and benzene (delocalized π ring) both have delocalized π electrons; cyclohexane does not, but the question only needs two. The other sets contain at most one such species (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> in B; O<sub>3</sub>, not O<sub>2</sub>, would be delocalized).

Propanoic acid can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water through its –COOH group and has a short hydrocarbon chain, so it is most soluble. Aldehydes only accept H bonds, and the longer-chain butanoic acid is less soluble.

In SCl<sub>4</sub>, S forms 4 bonds and has 1 lone pair, so it has 10 electrons around it: an expanded octet. PCl<sub>3</sub>, BF<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> all have exactly 8 electrons around the central atom.
"Van der Waals’ forces" describes dipole–dipole forces and London (dispersion) forces (plus dipole–induced dipole). Hydrogen bonding is treated as a separate, stronger intermolecular force.

NaHCO<sub>3</sub> contains the hydrogencarbonate ion, with delocalized π electrons over its O–C–O group, and benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, has a delocalized π ring. Cyclic or alkene hydrocarbons (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) and NaOH have no delocalization.

Each C in HC≡CH has 2 electron domains: linear, sp. B: C in C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> is tetrahedral, not square planar. C: N in NH<sub>3</sub> has 4 domains, not 3. D: O in water is sp<sup>3</sup>, not sp<sup>2</sup>.
Methanal contains a C=O double bond: two shared pairs = 4 electrons. Lone pairs on oxygen are not part of the bond.
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F in one molecule and a lone pair on N, O or F in the other. CH3OH and H2O both have O–H groups. CH4, CF4 and CH3OCH3 have no H on N/O/F.
Giant covalent structures (e.g. SiO2) have very high melting points, are insoluble in water and do not conduct even when molten: D. B is ionic (conducts when molten) and C is a metal.
ICl4− has 6 electron domains (4 bonding, 2 lone pairs) giving a square planar shape with 90° angles. AlCl4−, NH4+ and SiCl4 are all tetrahedral (109.5°).
Atom 1 (CH3 carbon, 4 domains) is sp3; atom 2 (C=O carbon, 3 domains) is sp2; atom 3 (the –OH oxygen: 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs) is sp3.

A very high melting point (1414 °C, silicon) with poor conductivity both solid and molten indicates a network (giant) covalent structure. An ionic lattice would conduct when molten; a metal conducts as a solid; simple molecules melt at low temperatures.
Bond polarity depends on electronegativity difference: Si (1.9) and F (4.0) differ by 2.1, the largest of the options (C–F 1.4, Si–Cl 1.3, C–Cl 0.6).
P in PH4+ has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so four electron domains give a tetrahedral shape and sp3 hybridization. Square planar needs six domains.
Every carbon is sp2 with 3 domains. π electrons: 6 in the ring + 2 in C=O = 8. σ bonds: 6 ring C–C + 5 C–H + 1 C–COOH + C=O(σ) + C–O + O–H = 15.
O3 (one single and one double O–O bond that can swap) and benzene (alternating C=C positions) have resonance structures. CO2 is fully described by O=C=O, so it has no significant resonance.
Urea has 4 N–H, 2 C–N and one C=O (2 pairs): 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 shared pairs = 16 bonding electrons. Lone pairs on N and O are non-bonding.
C6H12 (cyclohexane or a hexene) has no delocalized π system, so no resonance. PO43− can be drawn with the P=O in any of four positions, and benzene and O3 also have resonance structures.

π bonds come from sideways overlap of p orbitals, with electron density above and below (parallel to) the internuclear axis. They always form in addition to a σ bond, and σ bonds can also form from p or hybrid orbitals.

Propane cannot hydrogen bond; propanal can only accept H-bonds (C=O); propanol both donates and accepts via O–H; propanoic acid has both C=O and O–H. So: propane < propanal < propanol < propanoic acid.
Electronegativity differences: N–O 0.4, O–F 0.6, C–O 0.8, C–F 1.4. Increasing polarity: NO2 < OF2 < CO < CF4.

Methyl C: 4 bonds → sp3, tetrahedral. Carbonyl O: one double bond + 2 lone pairs = 3 domains → sp2, trigonal planar. The ring N with C=N and a lone pair has 3 domains → sp2, trigonal planar. Electron-domain geometry, not molecular shape, is asked.
σ: 6 ring C–C + 4 C–H + C–CN + C≡N (1 σ) + C–COOH + C=O (1 σ) + C–O + O–H = 16. π: 3 in the ring + 2 in C≡N + 1 in C=O = 6.
In diamond every C uses all four outer electrons in σ bonds (sp3), so there are no delocalized electrons and it does not conduct. Graphite, graphene and nanotubes have delocalized π electrons.
N in NO3− has three electron domains (resonance-delocalized bonds) and no lone pair, so it is trigonal planar with 120° angles.

Each contains a double bond on a carbon with three electron domains: the C=O carbon in CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (I) and CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> (II), and the C=C carbons in CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>2</sub>OH (III). All three have sp<sup>2</sup> atoms.

Methanal, H<sub>2</sub>C=O, has only one reasonable Lewis structure. Benzene, O<sub>3</sub> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> each need several resonance structures because their double bonds can be placed in different positions.
CH3OH has only a C–O single bond, the weakest and longest. CO has a triple bond, H2CO a double bond, and ethanoate has delocalized C–O bonds with a bond order of 1.5, so all of these are shorter.

The C in urea has three electron domains (C=O and two C–N) so it is trigonal planar. Each N has three bonds plus a lone pair, which is four domains, so the electron domain geometry is tetrahedral. The molecular shape at N would be trigonal pyramidal, but the question asks for electron domain geometry.
In SF4 sulfur forms four S–F bonds and keeps a lone pair: 10 electrons in its valence shell, which is an expanded octet. In SF2 sulfur has two bonds and two lone pairs, exactly 8 electrons.
Any overlap involving an s orbital is head-on along the bond axis, so s–s and s–p overlap can form only σ bonds. Two p orbitals can overlap head-on (σ) or sideways (π), so II is not "only sigma".

SO32− has three bonding domains and one lone pair on S, so it is trigonal pyramidal; PF3 is the same (3 bonds + 1 lone pair). BF3, SO3 and CO32− have no lone pair on the central atom and are trigonal planar.
Cl has 7 valence electrons; removing one for the + charge leaves 6. Two Cl–F bonds use 2 of these, leaving 4 electrons = 2 lone pairs, with 2 bonding pairs (a bent ion).

CH3CH2NH2 has an N–H bond, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, the strongest intermolecular force here. The others are polar but have no H bonded to N, O or F, so they have only dipole–dipole and London forces.
C=C has 1 σ + 1 π. Four C–C single bonds give 4 σ. Each of the four C≡N has 1 σ + 2 π. Total σ = 1 + 4 + 4 = 9; π = 1 + 8 = 9.
The circled CH3 carbon has four single bonds: sp3. The carbonyl O (double bond + 2 lone pairs, three domains) is sp2. The ring N with a C=N double bond and a lone pair has three domains: sp2.

All six H atoms in benzene are equivalent, so its 1H NMR spectrum shows one signal, and replacing any H gives the same, single C6H5Br. Benzene has delocalized (equal) C–C bonds and resists addition, so it does not decolourize bromine water.

Butane has only London forces (lowest). Propanone adds dipole–dipole forces. Propan-2-ol forms hydrogen bonds. Ethanoic acid forms stronger hydrogen bonds (it forms dimers) and has the highest b.p. Order: butane < propanone < propan-2-ol < ethanoic acid.
CO32− has resonance structures: the π electrons are delocalized over all three C–O bonds, so each has a bond order of 1⅓. OH−, H2CO and CO2 each have a single Lewis structure with localized bonds.
HC≡C–: both triple-bonded carbons are sp (2). CH2, CH2 and CH3 are sp3 (3). The C=O carbon is sp2 (1). Answer 3, 1, 2.

The false statement is C. Benzene's delocalized π system is very stable, so it usually undergoes substitution rather than addition (unlike alkenes). It is planar, with delocalized electrons and C–C bonds of bond order 1.5.
XeF4 has 6 electron domains (4 bonds + 2 lone pairs). The lone pairs sit opposite each other, leaving a square planar shape. SF4 (4 bonds + 1 lone pair) is see-saw, and CF4 and PF4+ are tetrahedral.
H–C≡N: the H–C single bond is 1 σ, and the C≡N triple bond is 1 σ + 2 π. Total 2 σ and 2 π.
In H2C=O, carbon has three electron domains (two C–H + C=O) so it is sp2. Oxygen has the double bond plus two lone pairs, three domains, so it is also sp2.
Carbon monoxide has a C≡O triple bond, the highest bond order and the shortest bond. CO2 and ethanal have C=O double bonds, and the ether has C–O single bonds (the longest).

Resonance structures are Lewis structures of the same species that differ only in where the electrons are placed, e.g. a double bond drawn in alternative positions (as in O3 or CO32−). The real structure is a hybrid with delocalized electrons.
SiO2 is a giant covalent (network) structure: each Si is bonded tetrahedrally to four O and each O to two Si. It is not made of discrete molecules, which is why its melting point is very high.
C in methanal (H2C=O) has three electron domains, so it is sp2. C in CO2 is sp (two domains), and N in CH3NH2 and O in H2O have four domains (sp3).
In SF6 sulfur forms six bonds, giving 12 electrons around it: an expanded octet. C in CO2, F in BF3 and O in H2O all have 8 electrons (B in BF3 would be the incomplete octet, not F).

SO<sub>2</sub> is a simple molecular substance with weak intermolecular forces, so it is the most volatile (a gas). SiO<sub>2</sub> is a covalent network and SnO<sub>2</sub>/SrO are giant ionic/high-melting solids.
HCN contains a C≡N triple bond; more shared electron pairs make a bond shorter and stronger. CH<sub>3</sub>CHNH has C=N; the amines have C–N single bonds.
Dispersion forces are generally weakest, then dipole–dipole, then hydrogen bonds; covalent bonds (intramolecular) are much stronger than any intermolecular force.
S in SCl<sub>4</sub> has four bonds plus one lone pair = 10 electrons (5 domains), an expanded octet. C in CO<sub>2</sub> and O in H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> obey the octet rule.
p1.flag: option D subscript cut off in image (P in PCl?); answer assumes PCl3

p1.key: In SiO2 (a covalent network) each Si is bonded to four O atoms with no lone pairs, so its electron domain geometry is tetrahedral. Don't confuse with molecular CO2 (linear).
CH<sub>4</sub> is a non-polar molecule (symmetrical tetrahedral), so the only forces between its molecules are London (dispersion) forces. Covalent bonds are within molecules, not between them.
Oxygen in H3O+ has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair: FC = 6 − 2 − ½(6) = +1.

SF4 has 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair (5 domains): electron domain geometry trigonal bipyramidal, but the molecular geometry is see-saw. Trigonal bipyramidal (B) is the domain geometry, not the shape.
In BF<sub>3</sub>, boron has only three bonding pairs (6 electrons), an incomplete octet. C, O and F in B and C have full octets; Cl in ClF<sub>3</sub> has an expanded octet.

CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> has the weakest IMFs (only weak dipole–dipole, low polarity); CH<sub>3</sub>CHO has stronger dipole–dipole forces from its C=O; CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH forms hydrogen bonds, so it has the highest boiling point.

All have 4 electron domains, but lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs: NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> (2 lone pairs, ≈105°) < NH<sub>3</sub> (1 lone pair, ≈107°) < NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (none, 109.5°).

In C, N carries the single unpaired electron (allowed for a radical, 17 valence electrons in total); formal charges are N +1, single-bonded O −1, double-bonded O 0. A gives N 9 electrons (invalid); B is valid but places +1 on the more electronegative oxygen, which is less favourable; D has too few electrons.
p1.flag: no ms; B and C both valid with equal |FC| – C chosen because + charge on less electronegative N
